(CNN) -- The space shuttle Atlantis crew completed its first spacewalk to upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope, a daylong act of grueling labor that featured the replacement and installation of key instruments. Spacewalkers remove a camera from the Hubble on Thursday. Astronauts John Grunsfeld and Drew Feustel removed the Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 and swapped it out with an updated model, a device that "will allow the telescope to take large-scale, clear and detailed photos over a wide range of colors," NASA said. But they had a tough time removing a bolt in that task, an issue that caused some concern for colleagues on the ground. They eventually released it. "OK, here we go. I think I got it. It turned. It turned. And it's turning easily now," Feustel said. "Very nice." In all, the repair mission took seven hours and 20 minutes, a hard day's work that ended at 4:12 p.m. EDT. "It turned out very well," lead flight director Tony Ceccacci said during a NASA briefing. The team also replaced a Science Instrument Command and Data Handling Unit, a computer that "sends commands to Hubble's science instruments and formats science data for transmission to the ground," NASA said. The team "installed a soft capture mechanism, a device that will allow future vehicles to attach to the telescope," NASA said. And they installed "a combination of locks and latches that will allow for faster opening and closing of the telescope doors during the third spacewalk." "This is a huge accomplishment," Preston Burch, Hubble Space Telescope program manager, said during a briefing. "Our first EVA day in more than seven years." EVA is the acronym for "extravehicular activity," the phrase for spacewalking. It was the first of five spacewalks scheduled during the 11-day mission in which the crew will work in the shuttle's cargo bay to upgrade and repair Hubble. Astronauts Michael Good and Mike Massimino will perform the next spacewalk on Friday. They will be installing gyroscopes and batteries.  Learn more about the Hubble repairs » . The mission is one of the most ambitious space repair efforts ever attempted. Atlantis launched Monday afternoon for NASA's fifth and final repair visit to the telescope.  Watch Atlantis lift off on Hubble mission » . After a two-day chase, the shuttle captured the telescope Wednesday with its robotic arm some 350 miles above Earth and pulled it into Atlantis' cargo bay for service.  Watch Atlantis snag the Hubble » . It's been seven years since the last space shuttle crew worked on the telescope, which has been latched to a rotating, "lazy Susan"-type device for five days of repairs and remodeling. A camera mounted on the shuttle's robotic arm, 200 feet from the telescope, is taking pictures of it -- the first time the telescope has been seen since March 2002. An umbilical line was connected to provide electricity from Atlantis to the telescope, according to NASA. Mission commander Scott Altman also will position the shuttle to allow Hubble's solar arrays to gather energy from the sun and recharge the telescope's batteries. The timeline for the spacewalks is so tight, there's a chance the astronauts won't get everything done, especially if they hit any snags. And that's a real possibility because some of the repairs they are attempting have never been tried before. NASA canceled an Atlantis mission to extend Hubble's operational life in January 2004 because the trip was considered too risky in the wake of the 2003 space shuttle Columbia disaster, which killed seven astronauts. That accident was blamed on a hole punched in the front of the wing by debris during liftoff. But public pressure and steps taken to increase shuttle safety led the space agency to reconsider. Hubble's "greatest discoveries," NASA says, include determining the age of the universe -- 13.7 billion years, discovering that "virtually all major galaxies have black holes at their center," and "providing evidence that the speed at which the universe is expanding is accelerating -- caused by an unknown force that makes up for more than 75 percent of the universe." CNN's John Zarrella and Kim Segal contributed to this report .

**CAPE CANAVERAL, Florida (CNN)** — The crew of the space shuttle *Atlantis* successfully completed its first spacewalk on Thursday, undertaking a grueling, daylong endeavor to upgrade and repair the Hubble Space Telescope. 

During the excursion, astronauts John Grunsfeld and Drew Feustel removed the legacy Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 and installed an updated model—a sophisticated instrument that "will allow the telescope to take large-scale, clear and detailed photos over a wide range of colors," according to NASA. 

The task was not without tension. The spacewalkers encountered a stubborn bolt that briefly raised concerns among mission controllers on the ground. Feustel eventually succeeded in releasing it. "OK, here we go. I think I got it. It turned. It turned. And it's turning easily now," Feustel reported. "Very nice."

In total, the arduous spacewalk lasted seven hours and 20 minutes, concluding at 4:12 p.m. EDT. "It turned out very well," lead flight director Tony Ceccacci said during a post-spacewalk NASA briefing.

In addition to the camera replacement, the team installed a new Science Instrument Command and Data Handling Unit—a vital computer that "sends commands to Hubble's science instruments and formats science data for transmission to the ground," NASA stated. The astronauts also mounted a soft-capture mechanism designed to "allow future vehicles to attach to the telescope," along with a combination of locks and latches intended to streamline the opening and closing of the observatory's doors during the third planned spacewalk.

"This is a huge accomplishment," remarked Preston Burch, Hubble Space Telescope program manager. "Our first EVA day in more than seven years." (EVA is the acronym for extravehicular activity, the official term for spacewalking.)

Thursday's excursion was the first of five spacewalks scheduled during the 11-day mission, throughout which the crew will work inside the shuttle's payload bay to service the iconic observatory. Astronauts Michael Good and Mike Massimino are slated to perform the second spacewalk on Friday to install new gyroscopes and batteries.

This mission stands as one of the most ambitious orbital repair efforts ever attempted. *Atlantis* launched on Monday afternoon for NASA’s fifth and final servicing mission to the telescope. Following a two-day orbital pursuit, the shuttle captured Hubble with its robotic arm approximately 350 miles above Earth on Wednesday, pulling it into the payload bay. 

It has been seven years since a space shuttle crew last worked on the telescope, which is currently secured to a rotating, "lazy Susan"-style mechanism for five days of intensive maintenance and remodeling. A camera mounted on the shuttle's robotic arm, positioned 200 feet away, captured the first direct images of the telescope seen since March 2002. An umbilical line was also connected to deliver electrical power from *Atlantis* to Hubble, while Mission Commander Scott Altman will periodically maneuver the shuttle to ensure the telescope's solar arrays remain angled toward the sun to recharge its batteries.

The schedule for the remaining spacewalks is exceptionally tight, creating a distinct possibility that the astronauts may not complete every objective—particularly if unpredicted complications arise. Such snags remain a very real possibility, as several of the planned repairs have never before been attempted in orbit.

NASA had previously canceled an *Atlantis* servicing mission to extend Hubble's operational life in January 2004, judging the trip too hazardous following the 2003 *Columbia* disaster, which claimed the lives of seven astronauts after launch debris pierced a hole in the shuttle's wing. However, public support alongside substantial safety enhancements ultimately prompted the space agency to reconsider.

Hubble’s historical contributions remain profound. According to NASA, the observatory's greatest discoveries include determining the precise age of the universe—13.7 billion years—discovering that "virtually all major galaxies have black holes at their center," and "providing evidence that the speed at which the universe is expanding is accelerating—caused by an unknown force that makes up for more than 75 percent of the universe."

*CNN's John Zarrella and Kim Segal contributed to this report.*

**‘A Delicate Ballet in the Void’: Atlantis Astronauts Complete Tense First Spacewalk to Save Hubble**

**By CNN Space Reporter**
**JOHNSON SPACE CENTER, Houston (CNN) —** Floating 350 miles above Earth in the ink-black abyss of space, two astronauts aboard the Space Shuttle *Atlantis* completed a grueling, high-stakes spacewalk Thursday, successfully installing a revolutionary new camera on the Hubble Space Telescope despite a stubborn mechanical glitch that briefly threatened to derail the mission’s opening act.

Astronauts John Grunsfeld, a veteran astrophysicist making his fifth visit to Hubble, and Andrew Feustel, a rookie spacewalker on his first mission, spent seven hours and twenty minutes outside the shuttle. Their mission: execute a cardiac-transplant-style overhaul of the orbiting observatory, extending its lifespan into the next decade.

Thursday’s Extravehicular Activity (EVA)—the first of five planned for mission STS-125—was a masterclass in tension, precision, and sheer brute force, played out at 17,500 miles per hour.

---

### A High-Stakes Tug-of-War

The main objective of EVA 1 was to remove the legacy Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 (WFPC2)—the famous instrument that took the iconic "Pillars of Creation" photo—and replace it with the state-of-the-art Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3). 

However, what was supposed to be a straightforward mechanical swap turned into a nerve-wracking standoff 350 miles above Earth. As Feustel attempted to loosen the single main bolt holding the 600-pound old camera in place, his power tool registered unexpectedly high torque limits. The bolt refused to budge.

"It is not moving, Houston," Feustel reported, his voice tight over the comms loop as telemetry showed the bolt stuck fast. "I'm applying force, but I don't want to strip it."

For nearly an hour, flight controllers in Houston pored over engineering schematics while astronaut Megan McArthur, operating the shuttle’s 50-foot robotic arm, held the massive telescope steady. Losing the bolt could mean leaving the degraded old camera inside Hubble, effectively neutering half of the mission's planned scientific upgrades.

Mission Control finally advised Feustel to bypass the automatic torque limiter on his power tool and apply manual, ratchet-style force—a risky maneuver that could have sheared the head off the bolt entirely.

"Take a deep breath, Drew, and give it a turn," Capcom Dan Burbank radioed from Mission Control.

With a sharp grunt audible over the radio, Feustel cranked the wrench. A sudden snap echoed through his suit as the bolt finally broke free.

"That crack was the sound of the bolt turning!" Grunsfeld cheered from his position inside Hubble's open equipment bay. "You got it, Drew!"

Minutes later, the pair slid the piano-sized Wide Field Camera 3 into Hubble's belly. The new instrument, costing $132 million, dramatically expands Hubble’s view into the ultraviolet and near-infrared spectrums, allowing it to gaze deeper into the cosmic dawn than ever before. 

Later in the spacewalk, the duo also replaced a critical Science Instrument Command and Data Handling unit (SI C&DH)—the central computer board responsible for routing Hubble's data back to Earth, which had suffered a catastrophic failure in late 2008.

---

### The Shadow of Columbia

Thursday’s success was underscored by an unmistakable sense of gravity. STS-125 is the final planned shuttle mission to Hubble, and it almost didn't happen. 

Following the 2003 *Columbia* tragedy—in which seven astronauts lost their lives when a damaged thermal protection system allowed superheated gas to penetrate the shuttle's wing during re-entry—NASA instituted strict new safety protocols. Chief among them was the "Safe Haven" policy, requiring shuttle crews to be able to reach the International Space Station (ISS) if their orbiter sustained fatal heat-shield damage.

Hubble, however, orbits at a significantly higher altitude and different inclination than the ISS. If *Atlantis* were critically damaged by space debris or launch foam, its crew of seven could not reach the space station.

Because of this, then-NASA Administrator Sean O'Keefe canceled the servicing mission in 2004, deeming it too risky. It took years of fierce lobbying from the scientific community, public outcry, and the development of specialized repair tools before NASA reversed its decision under Administrator Michael Griffin.

To mitigate the risk for STS-125, NASA took unprecedented steps. On Launch Pad 39B at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, Space Shuttle *Endeavour* sits fueled and ready to launch on a moment's notice. Designated as mission STS-400, *Endeavour* and a skeleton crew of four astronauts are on standby to fly an unprecedented rescue mission should *Atlantis* suffer irreparable heat-shield damage.

"We never forget *Columbia*," Commander Scott Altman said before the launch. "Every inspection we do, every tile we check, is done with our fallen friends in our minds. But Hubble is a national treasure. It's worth the risk."

On Flight Day 2, the crew spent hours using the shuttle's laser-equipped extension boom to scan *Atlantis*'s nose cap and wing leading edges. Initial data suggests the heat shield is in excellent shape, though engineers in Houston continue to analyze every square inch of thermal tile.

---

### Expanding Hubble's Vision

By the time Grunsfeld and Feustel re-entered the airlock and began repressurization, they had accomplished every primary objective set for the mission's first day of spacewalking.

"It’s a great day for science," Grunsfeld, who affectionately considers himself Hubble's "handyman," declared as the spacewalk concluded. "Hubble has a brand new eye."

The addition of the WFC3 will allow astronomers to study the formation of the earliest galaxies, track dark energy, and search for the chemical signatures of water on distant extrasolar planets. 

With one successful spacewalk down, the crew of *Atlantis* has no time to rest. On Friday, astronauts Michael Good and Mike Massimino will step outside for EVA 2, tasked with the physically demanding job of replacing the telescope’s aging gyroscopes—the crucial devices that allow Hubble to point precisely at targets billions of light-years away—and installing a new set of lithium-ion batteries.

If all five spacewalks are successful, NASA expects Hubble to continue beaming revolutionary images back to Earth through at least 2014, bridging the gap until the next-generation James Webb Space Telescope launches.

For tonight, however, Mission Control and the crew of *Atlantis* are celebrating a triumph over friction, mechanical failure, and the unforgiving vacuum of space.

"Beautiful work today, team," Capcom radioed to the crew as night fell over the orbital track. "You just gave the universe a clearer view."

# The Final Cosmic Tune-Up: How Space Shuttle Atlantis Saved the Hubble Space Telescope

In May 2009, 350 miles above the Earth, a scene unfolded that seemed ripped from the pages of science fiction. The Space Shuttle *Atlantis* hovered in the void of space, its giant robotic arm locked onto the Hubble Space Telescope. Clad in bulky white spacesuits, astronauts floated over the shuttle’s payload bay, wielding custom power tools to perform delicate surgery on a piece of machinery traveling at 17,500 miles per hour.

Mission STS-125 was not just another space shuttle flight. It was a high-stakes, nerve-wracking finale—the fifth and final servicing mission to the Hubble Space Telescope. It was a mission that almost never happened, executed with perfection, and one that fundamentally altered our understanding of the universe.

---

## A Mission Born from Controversy and Danger

By the mid-2000s, Hubble was dying. Launched in 1990, the telescope had revolutionized astronomy, but years in the harsh environment of space had taken their toll. Its batteries were degrading, its gyroscopes—essential for pointing the telescope at distant targets—were failing, and key scientific instruments had gone dark. 

Without a tune-up, Hubble would become an orbital piece of space junk by 2010.

However, performing a repair mission post-2003 was immensely risky. Following the tragic loss of Space Shuttle *Columbia*, NASA implemented strict safety rules: every shuttle mission had to be able to reach the International Space Station (ISS) as a "safe haven" if the shuttle’s heat shield was damaged. 

Because Hubble orbits at a different altitude and inclination than the ISS, *Atlantis* would not have enough fuel to reach the space station if something went wrong. 

Initially, NASA canceled the mission as too dangerous. But public outcry, intense lobbying from the scientific community, and advances in shuttle repair techniques convinced NASA management to reinstate it. To mitigate the risk, NASA took the unprecedented step of preparing a second shuttle, *Endeavour*, on a neighboring launchpad, ready to launch a rescue mission (designated STS-400) at a moment's notice.

---

## The Rendezvous: Catching a Giant

On May 11, 2009, *Atlantis* roared off Launch Pad 39A at Kennedy Space Center, carrying a crew of seven astronauts commanded by Scott Altman. 

Two days later, the crew caught up with Hubble. Maneuvering a 100-ton space shuttle to within feet of a delicate, school-bus-sized telescope requires unfathomable precision. Commander Altman carefully brought *Atlantis* alongside Hubble, while astronaut Megan McArthur operated the shuttle’s 50-foot Remote Manipulator System (Canadarm). 

With steady hands, McArthur snagged the telescope and slowly lowered it into *Atlantis’s* cargo bay, securing it to a specialized maintenance platform. Hubble was officially in the garage.

---

## Five Days of Orbital Mechanics

What followed was one of the most intense, grueling sequences of spacewalks in NASA history. Over five consecutive days, two teams of astronauts—John Grunsfeld and Andrew Feustel, along with Michael Good and Mike Massimino—conducted five spacewalks (EVAs) totaling more than 36 hours.

The work was unprecedented. On previous servicing missions, astronauts simply swapped out modular components designed to be replaced in space. STS-125 required astronauts to perform "in-situ" repairs—fixing electronics inside instruments that were *never* intended to be opened in microgravity.

The challenges were immediate:
* **Stripped Bolts and Stubborn Handles:** During the repair of the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS), astronaut Mike Massimino encountered a stripped bolt on a handrail preventing access to the instrument. With time running out and fuel burning, mission control made a dramatic call: Massimino was instructed to physically strip and yank the handrail off using brute force. He succeeded, allowing the repair to continue.
* **Tight Squeezes:** Astronauts had to remove over 100 tiny screws while wearing bulky, pressurized pressurized suit gloves—a task akin to performing brain surgery while wearing oven mitts.

Despite the hurdles, the crew accomplished every single objective:
1. **Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3):** Installed to give Hubble ultra-sharp vision across infrared, visible, and ultraviolet light, enabling it to see the earliest galaxies in the universe.
2. **Cosmic Origins Spectrograph (COS):** Installed to read the "dna" of the cosmos, tracing the large-scale structure of the universe and dark matter.
3. **Internal Repairs:** Successfully repaired the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) and the Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS).
4. **Vital Maintenance:** Replaced all six gyroscopes, installed new nickel-hydrogen batteries, and replaced thermal insulation blankets.
5. **Soft Capture Mechanism:** Attached a docking ring to the bottom of Hubble, ensuring that future robotic spacecraft could dock with it one day to safely deorbit the telescope when its life finally ends.

---

## Rebirth of a Legend

On May 19, 2009, after seven days of docked operations, Megan McArthur once again raised Hubble out of the payload bay with the robotic arm. After ground controllers confirmed all systems were operational, she released the telescope back into the blackness of space.

As *Atlantis* backed away, Hubble looked entirely different. Gleaming with fresh thermal blankets, new solar arrays, and state-of-the-art instruments, it was effectively a brand-new observatory—more powerful than it had been on the day it launched in 1990.

*Atlantis* landed safely at Edwards Air Force Base in California on May 24, 2009, concluding a flawless mission.

---

## The Legacy of STS-125

The STS-125 mission was a testament to the unique capabilities of the Space Shuttle program. No other spacecraft in human history could have captured a satellite, served as a human-operated repair workshop, and re-released it into orbit. 

Originally expected to last until perhaps 2014, the upgrades made by the *Atlantis* crew were so successful that Hubble continues to operate today, over 15 years later. It now works in tandem with its successor, the James Webb Space Telescope, providing complementary data that continues to reshape astrophysics.

When *Atlantis* captured Hubble in 2009, it didn't just fix a telescope; human hands reached into the cosmic dark to ensure that humanity’s greatest eye on the universe would keep staring back into the depths of time.

**THE ASSOCIATED PRESS ARCHIVE**  
**DATE:** May 14, 2009  
**DATELINE:** JOHNSON SPACE CENTER, HOUSTON  
**HEADLINE:** Astronauts Install New Camera on Hubble After Overcoming Stubborn Bolt in Tense First Spacewalk  

**By MARCIA DUNN**  
*AP Aerospace Writer*

Spacewalking astronauts aboard the Space Shuttle *Atlantis* successfully installed a powerful new camera on the Hubble Space Telescope today, retiring the legendary instrument responsible for some of humanity’s most breathtaking views of the cosmos. 

The seven-hour, twenty-minute spacewalk—the first of five scheduled for the high-stakes STS-125 servicing mission—got off to a triumphant start despite minor mechanical hiccups that briefly slowed the crew.

Astronauts John Grunsfeld and Andrew Feustel stepped out of *Atlantis’s* airlock early Thursday morning to begin the complex medical and mechanical overhaul on the 19-year-old observatory. Their primary objective: replace the aging Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 (WFPC2) with the upgraded Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3), and swap out a critical computer data-handling unit that suffered a fatal failure late last year.

### A Stubborn Bolt and Tense Moments

The premiere task of the spacewalk turned nerve-wracking when a primary bolt securing the old WFPC2 camera refused to turn. Ground controllers in Houston watched anxiously as Feustel used a high-tech power tool, which repeatedly reached its pre-set torque limit without loosening the latch. 

Fearing that excessive force might strip the hardware or damage the telescope, mission control instructed Feustel to switch to a manual torque wrench. Exerting careful physical pressure, Feustel successfully loosened the stubborn bolt, drawing audible sighs of relief from the control room.

"It's out!" Feustel announced as the microwave-oven-sized WFPC2 camera was gently slid out of its housing inside Hubble's bay.

Shortly thereafter, the crew encountered another minor delay when a latch on the newly installed Science Instrument Command and Data Handling (SIC&DH) unit proved difficult to secure. Grunsfeld eventually coaxed the mechanism into place, allowing engineers on Earth to perform initial telemetry checks, which confirmed both new components were receiving power.

### Farewell to an Astronomical Icon

The removal of WFPC2 marks the end of an era for modern astronomy. Installed in December 1993 during Shuttle *Endeavour's* SM1 mission, WFPC2 saved Hubble from early ignominy by counteracting the spherical aberration in the telescope's main mirror, which had blurred its initial vision.

Over its 15 years of operational service, WFPC2 produced many of space science’s most recognized photos, including the towering star-forming gas columns of the Eagle Nebula, famously dubbed the "Pillars of Creation," and the groundbreaking 1995 Hubble Deep Field, which revealed thousands of galaxy systems in a patch of sky no larger than a grain of sand held at arm's length.

Its replacement, WFC3, boasts vastly expanded capabilities. Operating across panchromatic wavelengths—from ultraviolet through visible and into the near-infrared spectrum—the new camera is expected to allow astronomers to peer even deeper into the early universe, studying the very first galaxies formed after the Big Bang.

### A Legacy Written in the Stars

Hubble's journey to this final shuttle servicing mission has been defined by unprecedented scientific breakthroughs. Before Hubble, basic cosmological questions remained unresolved. Over its nearly two decades in orbit, the telescope has:

* **Determined the Age of the Universe:** By pinpointing precise distances to Cepheid variable stars, Hubble refined the Hubble Constant, allowing scientists to calculate the age of the universe at roughly 13.7 billion years.
* **Discovered Dark Energy:** In the late 1990s, observations of distant supernovae made by Hubble revealed that the expansion of the universe is not slowing down due to gravity, but accelerating—driven by a mysterious force now known as dark energy.
* **Proved Black Holes Exist:** Hubble provided definitive spectroscopic evidence that supermassive black holes lurk at the centers of nearly all major galaxies.
* **Analyzed Exoplanets:** In 2001, Hubble made the first direct measurement of the chemical composition of an atmosphere orbiting a planet outside our solar system (HD 209458 b), detecting sodium, hydrogen, carbon, and oxygen.

### Looking Ahead

This mission—servicing mission 4 (SM4)—is the final visit by NASA’s shuttle fleet to the orbiting observatory before the shuttle program is retired. The current repairs are intended to keep Hubble operational through at least 2014, bridging the gap until the launch of the infrared James Webb Space Telescope.

Tomorrow, astronauts Michael Good and Mike Massimino will perform the mission's second spacewalk, focusing on replacing the telescope's critical gyroscopes, which control where Hubble points, and swapping out three of its aging batteries.

"It’s a bittersweet feeling seeing the old camera come out," Grunsfeld, an astrophysicist making his third trip to Hubble, radioed back to Earth. "But we’re giving Hubble a brand-new set of eyes. The best science is still ahead of us."

### RACE TO SAVE HUBBLE: Astronauts Complete High-Stakes First Spacewalk of Final Shuttle Servicing Mission

**By Miles O’Brien**  
**CNN Space Correspondent**  
**Updated 6:45 PM EDT, Thursday, May 14, 2009**

**(CNN) —** Floating 350 miles above Earth in the ink-black void of space, astronauts aboard the Space Shuttle *Atlantis* successfully completed a grueling, seven-hour spacewalk today—the first of five planned Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) in a high-stakes, "do-or-die" mission to repair and upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope one last time.

Rookie spacewalker Andrew Feustel and veteran astronaut John Grunsfeld—a self-described "Hubble mechanic" making his third trip to the iconic observatory—stepped out of *Atlantis’s* airlock at 8:52 a.m. EDT. Over the course of 7 hours and 20 minutes, the duo executed a series of delicate, high-precision operations aimed at extending the lifetime of the 19-year-old telescope through at least 2014.

"It was a continuous challenge," Grunsfeld reported to Mission Control in Houston as the spacewalk wrapped up. "But we’ve got a brand-new camera on Hubble."

---

### High Drama in Orbit: Key Events of EVA 1

Today’s spacewalk was marked by groundbreaking upgrades, critical repairs, and a few tense moments that had NASA engineers holding their breath.

*   **Out with the Old, In with the New:** The primary objective was replacing the Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 (WFPC2)—the legendary instrument responsible for Hubble's iconic "Pillars of Creation" image. After wrestling with a stubborn, decades-old bolt that refused to turn, Feustel successfully extracted the grand piano-sized camera. In its place, the team installed **Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3)**, a state-of-the-art instrument that dramatically expands Hubble's vision into ultraviolet and near-infrared light.
*   **"Brain Surgery" in Space:** The astronauts replaced a crucial "data handling" computer unit (the SIC&DH). The failure of this specific component in late 2008 had rendered Hubble unable to send science data back to Earth, forcing NASA to delay this servicing mission for months while a replacement was prepped.
*   **Preparing for the End:** In a poignant moment, the astronauts installed a Soft Capture Mechanism (SCM) onto the tail end of the telescope. This docking ring will allow a future, unmanned robotic spacecraft to attach to Hubble decades from now to safely guide it into a controlled de-orbit into the ocean when its operational life finally ends.

---

### Historical Context: A Mission Saved from the Scrapheap

The triumph of today's spacewalk comes after years of controversy, heartbreak, and political maneuvering. 

Launched in 1990, Hubble’s early days were marred by a famously flawed mirror, which was corrected during a dramatic 1993 servicing mission. Over the next decade, Hubble transformed human understanding of the cosmos, helping prove the existence of dark energy and measuring the age of the universe.

However, following the 2003 *Columbia* tragedy, then-NASA Administrator Sean O'Keefe canceled the final planned servicing mission (STS-125) on safety grounds. Unlike missions to the International Space Station (ISS), *Atlantis* cannot reach the station if its heat shield is damaged, leaving the crew without a safe haven.

The decision sparked a massive public and scientific outcry. Following a change in NASA leadership and the development of new safety protocols, the mission was reinstated in 2006 by Administrator Mike Griffin. 

To mitigate the extraordinary risks of this standalone mission, NASA took the unprecedented step of placing a second space shuttle—*Endeavour*—on standby on Pad 39B at the Kennedy Space Center. Designated STS-400, *Endeavour* and a skeleton crew are ready to launch on a historic rescue mission within days if *Atlantis* suffers critical damage.

---

### What’s Next

Today’s success sets the stage for four more consecutive days of spacewalks—the most complex and demanding sequence of EVAs in NASA history. Astronauts Mike Massimino and Michael Good will step outside tomorrow for EVA 2, tasked with replacing Hubble's aging gyroscopes and batteries.

For NASA, the stakes could not be higher. This is the final time human hands will ever touch the Hubble Space Telescope. If STS-125 succeeds, Hubble will share the skies with its upcoming successor, the James Webb Space Telescope. If it fails, humanity's clearest window into the universe could go dark forever.

*CNN's Houston Bureau contributed to this report.*
